doc.title: Chris Parker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 5, 2023

title: Learning dynamics from playing for strippers and singers
summary: Parker learned dynamics from Ellington at Newport and from backing strippers and singers, and says playing must reflect a song's emotion, citing Ray Charles tunes.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: I have a feeling, this is just a guess, but that you were aware of almost all that material that you just mentioned by the time you really started playing out. Is that a fair statement?

I didn’t know the Italian words for it, you know musical words, but I knew crescendo and decrescendo and “Dimuendo and Crescendo in Blue” that Duke Ellington tune from a “Live at Newport” concert — you know those are the first two ones that I learned. And I listened to that record over and over and over again with Paul Gonsalves, 40 choruses on the blues, and Jo Jones, you know rapping a newspaper on the stage. That’s a great record. Anyway by the time I was backing up strippers I knew that they have to be brought on, they have to be introduced, they have to — you have to let the audience know that the dancers are here and if they’ve got something to say over the microphone or one of them — we had singers too — if the singers — you’ve got to come down for the singers so the audience can hear what she’s singing. Those things I learned pretty soon from playing with that band, and adapted it to everything I did subsequently, you know, dynamics, and listening to what’s going on, listening to the singer, listening to the horn player, listening to the sections of the tune, listening to the whole song itself. What’s the song about? Is it “Rainy Days and Mondays” or is it you know something more raucous you know. “Rock House” or, oh jeez.
Yeah I’m thinking of a Ray Charles tune, “Tell the Truth.”

Oh my God that’s one of my favorites, and “Hit the Road, Jack” you know has it got some grit to it? Is the singer expressing anger? Disappointment or melancholy? So all those emotional feelings have got to be incorporated into your playing as well.
